questions.subtopic: Location, Capacity, Unit of Transfer & Access Methods
questions.concept: Four Memory Access Methods
questions.question: According to Slide 13 ('Characteristics of memory systems: Access Method'), which memory access method is matched with its correct hardware example?
options: Sequential access: magnetic tape; Direct access: magnetic disk; Random access: RAM; Associative access: cache memory
Sequential access: RAM; Direct access: CPU registers; Random access: magnetic tape; Associative access: CD-ROM
Sequential access: cache; Direct access: SRAM; Random access: magnetic disk; Associative access: magnetic tape
All four memory types use purely sequential access
questions.explanationEn: Slide 13 defines the four access methods: Sequential access (example: tape), Direct access (jumping to general vicinity plus sequential search; example: disk), Random access (example: RAM), and Associative access (example: cache).
questions.explanationVi: Slide 13 (trang 6) phân loại 4 phương pháp truy cập bộ nhớ: Truy cập tuần tự (Sequential: băng từ/tape), Truy cập trực tiếp (Direct: đĩa từ/disk), Truy cập ngẫu nhiên (Random: RAM), và Truy cập liên kết (Associative: bộ nhớ đệm cache).

questions.subtopic: Memory Hierarchy Pyramid (Cost, Speed, Size)
questions.concept: Memory Hierarchy trade-offs
questions.question: As you move UP the Memory Hierarchy pyramid from Off-line Storage (Magnetic Tape) toward Inboard Memory and CPU Registers (Slides 15–16), how do cost per bit, access speed, and storage capacity change?
options: Cost per bit decreases, access speed decreases, and total capacity increases
Cost per bit increases, access speed increases (access time decreases), and total capacity (size) decreases
Cost per bit increases, access speed decreases, and total capacity increases
Cost per bit, access speed, and capacity all remain constant across every level
questions.explanationEn: Slides 15–16 show that moving up the pyramid (Magnetic Tape -> Magnetic Disk -> Main Memory -> Cache -> Register) results in Increasing Cost Per Bit, Increasing Speed, and Decreasing Size (capacity).
questions.explanationVi: Theo tháp phân cấp bộ nhớ (Slide 15–16): Khi đi từ đáy tháp (Băng từ, Đĩa từ) lên đỉnh tháp (RAM, Cache, Thanh ghi), chi phí trên mỗi bit tăng lên, tốc độ truy cập tăng lên, nhưng dung lượng lưu trữ giảm xuống.

questions.subtopic: Temporal, Spatial & Algorithmic Locality
questions.concept: Temporal vs. Spatial Locality of Reference
questions.question: How does 'Spatial Locality' differ from 'Temporal Locality' in cache memory design (Slide 21)?
options: Temporal locality states that a recently referenced memory item is likely to be referenced again in the near future; Spatial locality states that if a memory location is referenced, nearby addresses in its neighborhood are likely to be referenced soon (justifying fetching an entire block into cache)
Temporal locality fetches adjacent blocks from disk; Spatial locality flushes the cache on every clock cycle
Temporal locality only applies to magnetic tape; Spatial locality only applies to CPU status flags
Spatial locality means instructions are executed in reverse alphabetical order
questions.explanationEn: Slide 21 defines Temporal locality ('a memory content referenced will be referenced again in the near future') and Spatial locality ('if a memory content has been referenced, its neighborhood will be referenced as well in the near future—save the block of memory around X in cache').
questions.explanationVi: Slide 21 phân biệt: Tính cục bộ về thời gian (Temporal locality) là một ô nhớ vừa được truy cập sẽ có khả năng cao được truy cập lại trong tương lai gần; Tính cục bộ về không gian (Spatial locality) là các ô nhớ lân cận xung quanh nó cũng sẽ sớm được truy cập (do đó cache nạp cả một khối/block).

questions.subtopic: SRAM vs. DRAM Cell Structure & Trade-offs
questions.concept: Comparing DRAM and SRAM properties
questions.question: According to the 'Summary: DRAM vs SRAM' table (Slide 30, p. 11 of `ch03_Internal_External.pdf`), which statement accurately contrasts DRAM and SRAM?
options: DRAM uses 1 capacitor + 1 transistor per bit, requires periodic refresh (every 4–8 ms), has destructive reads (requiring write-back so access time < cycle time), and multiplexes address lines; SRAM uses 1 flip-flop (4–6 transistors) per bit, has non-destructive reads (access time = cycle time), and is 8–16x faster
DRAM uses 6 transistors per bit and never needs refreshing; SRAM uses 1 capacitor and requires refresh every 4 ms
DRAM is used for L1/L2 caches and TLBs; SRAM is used for high-density main memory modules
SRAM multiplexes row and column addresses on the same pins, whereas DRAM uses destructive reads
questions.explanationEn: Slide 30 in `ch03_Internal_External.pdf` summarizes: DRAM (main memory, 1 capacitor + 1 transistor/bit, refresh every 4–8 ms, destructive read requiring write-back so access time < cycle time, 25–50x denser, multiplexed address lines) vs. SRAM (caches/TLB, 1 flip-flop of 4–6 transistors/bit, non-destructive read so access time = cycle time, 8–16x faster, non-multiplexed address lines).
questions.explanationVi: Theo bảng tổng kết Slide 30 (`ch03_Internal_External.pdf`): DRAM dùng 1 tụ điện + 1 transistor/bit, cần làm tươi mỗi 4–8 ms, đọc hủy dữ liệu (cần ghi lại nên access time < cycle time), và dồn kênh địa chỉ; còn SRAM dùng flip-flop 4–6 transistor/bit, đọc không hủy dữ liệu (access time = cycle time), nhanh gấp 8–16 lần và dùng làm Cache.

questions.subtopic: ROM Family (MROM, PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, Flash)
questions.concept: Comparing EPROM, EEPROM, and Flash Memory
questions.question: According to Table 5.1 ('Semiconductor Memory Types', Slide 7 of `ch03_Internal_External.pdf`), how do EPROM, EEPROM, and Flash memory differ in their erasure mechanism and granularity?
options: EPROM is erased electrically at the byte-level; EEPROM is erased with UV light; Flash cannot be erased
EPROM is erased using UV light at the chip-level; EEPROM is erased electrically at the byte-level; Flash memory is erased electrically at the block-level
All three are volatile read-write memories that lose data when power is removed
EPROM uses masks at manufacture; EEPROM erases entire blocks only; Flash erases individual bits with UV light
questions.explanationEn: Table 5.1 (p. 4 of `ch03_Internal_External.pdf`) categorizes EPROM, EEPROM, and Flash as non-volatile 'Read-mostly memory': EPROM erases via 'UV light, chip-level'; EEPROM erases 'Electrically, byte-level'; Flash memory erases 'Electrically, block-level'.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Bảng 5.1 (Slide 7, `ch03_Internal_External.pdf`): EPROM xóa bằng tia cực tím (UV light) ở mức toàn chip (chip-level); EEPROM xóa bằng điện ở mức từng byte (byte-level); còn Flash memory xóa bằng điện ở mức khối (block-level).

questions.subtopic: Word Alignment & Byte Ordering (Big-Endian vs. Little-Endian)
questions.concept: Big-Endian vs. Little-Endian Byte Ordering in Memory
questions.question: A 32-bit (4-byte) integer `0xA1B2C3D4` is stored in memory starting at byte address `0x100` (`0x100`, `0x101`, `0x102`, `0x103`). What are the byte values stored at addresses `0x100`, `0x101`, `0x102`, and `0x103` on an x86-64 system (Little-Endian) versus a SPARC system (Big-Endian)?
options: Both architectures store `A1 B2 C3 D4` in identical order from `0x100` to `0x103`
questions.explanationEn: Slide 12 (`ch03_Internal_External.pdf`) shows that in Big-Endian (SPARC, z/Architecture), the least significant byte (`D4`) has the highest address (`0x103`), so `0x100..0x103` holds `a1 b2 c3 d4`. In Little-Endian (x86, x86-64), the least significant byte (`D4`) has the lowest address (`0x100`), so `0x100..0x103` holds `d4 c3 b2 a1`.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 12 (`ch03_Internal_External.pdf`): Với Little-Endian (x86, x86-64), byte có trọng số thấp nhất (`D4`) nằm ở địa chỉ thấp nhất (`0x100`), nên từ `0x100` đến `0x103` lần lượt là `D4, C3, B2, A1`. Với Big-Endian (SPARC), byte có trọng số cao nhất (`A1`) nằm ở địa chỉ thấp nhất (`0x100`), nên lần lượt là `A1, B2, C3, D4`.

questions.subtopic: 2D DRAM Bank, Supercells & RAS/CAS Pin Multiplexing
questions.concept: DRAM 2D Matrix Address Pin Multiplexing (16Mbit Chip = 4M x 4)
questions.question: As shown on Slides 41–42 of `ch03_Internal_External.pdf` (Figure 5.3: Typical 16-Mbit DRAM organized as `4M × 4`), the memory array is organized as a `2048 × 2048 × 4-bit` square matrix using row/column address multiplexing (`RAS` and `CAS`). How many physical address pins (`A0` to `A_k`) are required on the chip package to address all `4M` (2^22) 4-bit supercells, and what happens to chip capacity if 1 more address pin is added?
options: 22 address pins (A0–A21); adding 1 more address pin doubles (×2) chip capacity
4 address pins (A0–A3); adding 1 more address pin increases capacity by 4 bits
16 address pins (A0–A15); adding 1 more address pin has no effect on capacity
11 address pins (A0–A10, since 2^11 = 2048 rows and 2048 columns); adding 1 more address pin doubles both row and column ranges, quadrupling (×4) chip capacity
questions.explanationEn: Slide 41 states: 'A 16Mbit chip can be organised as a 2048 x 2048 x 4bit array -> Reduces number of address pins -> Multiplex row address and column address -> 11 pins to address (2^11 = 2048) -> Adding one more pin doubles range of values so x4 capacity.'
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 41–42 (`ch03_Internal_External.pdf`): Chip DRAM 16Mbit (`4M × 4`) được tổ chức thành ma trận vuông `2048 × 2048 × 4 bit`. Nhờ dồn kênh địa chỉ hàng (RAS) và cột (CAS), chip chỉ cần 11 chân địa chỉ (`A0–A10`, vì 2^11 = 2048). Khi thêm 1 chân địa chỉ, cả số hàng và số cột đều tăng gấp đôi nên dung lượng chip tăng gấp 4 lần (×4).
questions.formula: Rows = Cols = 2^pins; Total_Supercells = 2^pins * 2^pins = 2^(2*pins)
questions.stepByStep:
1. Array size = 2048 rows × 2048 columns = 2^11 × 2^11 = 2^22 (4M) supercells.
2. Multiplexing row and column addresses uses 11 pins (A0–A10).
3. Adding 1 pin -> 12 pins -> 2^12 × 2^12 = 2^24 (4× capacity).

questions.subtopic: Low-Order, High-Order & Mixed Memory Interleaving
questions.concept: Mixed Memory Interleaving 6-Bit Address Decoding (Slide 47)
questions.question: On Slide 47 ('Mixed Interleaving', p. 20 of `ch03_Internal_External.pdf`), a 6-bit Memory Address Register (`b5 b4 b3 b2 b1 b0`) is partitioned so that the most significant 2 bits (`b5 b4`) specify the Bank address, the next 3 bits (`b3 b2 b1`) specify the Word address within the bank, and the least significant bit (`b0`) specifies the Module (parity) within the bank: `(Bank, Word, Module)`. For decimal address `6` (`000110_2`) and decimal address `41` (`101001_2`), what are their `(Bank, Word, Module)` coordinates?
options: Address 6 = (1, 3, 0); Address 41 = (1, 4, 2)
Address 6 = (0, 6, 0); Address 41 = (2, 5, 0)
Address 6 = (0, 3, 0); Address 41 = (2, 4, 1)
Address 6 = (3, 0, 0); Address 41 = (4, 2, 1)
questions.explanationEn: Slide 47 explicitly works out both examples: 6 = 000110_2 = (00_2, 011_2, 0_2) = (0, 3, 0), so address 6 is in Bank 0, Word 3, Module M0. And 41 = 101001_2 = (10_2, 100_2, 1_2) = (2, 4, 1), so address 41 is in Bank 2, Word 4, Module M5.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 47: Địa chỉ 6-bit được tách thành (2 bit cao: Bank, 3 bit giữa: Word, 1 bit thấp LSB: Module).
questions.formula: (Bank, Word, Module) = (A[5:4], A[3:1], A[0])

questions.subtopic: Logical (Virtual) vs. Physical Cache Addressing
questions.concept: Logical (Virtual) Cache vs. Physical Cache
questions.question: Where is a 'Logical Cache' (Virtual Cache) positioned relative to the processor and the Memory Management Unit (MMU), and what are its primary advantage and disadvantage compared to a Physical Cache?
options: It sits between the MMU and main memory; it is slower than physical cache but never needs flushing
It sits inside the magnetic disk controller and stores LBA sector numbers

It sits between the processor and the MMU, storing data using virtual addresses; cache access is faster because it responds before MMU address translation, but the cache must be flushed (or tagged) on each context switch because different applications share the same virtual address space
It replaces the ALU and translates assembly code into C++
questions.explanationEn: Slides 32–33 (`ch03_CacheMemory.pdf`) explain that a Logical (virtual) cache sits between the Processor and the MMU and stores data using virtual addresses. Its advantage is faster access (before MMU translation), and its disadvantage is that virtual addresses use the same address space across applications, requiring a cache flush on each context switch.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 32–33 (`ch03_CacheMemory.pdf`): Cache logic (Virtual cache) nằm giữa CPU và bộ quản lý bộ nhớ ảo (MMU), dùng địa chỉ ảo nên truy cập nhanh hơn (không cần đợi MMU dịch địa chỉ), nhưng có nhược điểm là phải xóa (flush) cache mỗi khi chuyển ngữ cảnh (context switch).

questions.subtopic: Direct Mapping Address Structure & Hex Examples
questions.concept: Direct Mapping Bit Partitioning (64KB Cache, 4B Block, 16MB Memory)
questions.question: In the benchmark example on Slides 36 and 42 (`ch03_CacheMemory.pdf`), a system has a 16 MB main memory (byte-addressable, 24-bit address) and a 64 KB Direct-Mapped cache with a block (line) size of 4 bytes. How many cache lines does the cache have, and how is the 24-bit physical address partitioned into `(Tag, Line/Slot, Word)` bits?
options: 64K (2^16) cache lines; Tag = 6 bits, Line/Slot = 16 bits, Word = 2 bits
4K (2^12) cache lines; Tag = 10 bits, Line/Slot = 12 bits, Word = 2 bits
16K (2^14) cache lines; Tag = 9 bits, Line/Slot = 13 bits, Word = 2 bits
16K (2^14) cache lines; Tag = 8 bits, Line/Slot = 14 bits, Word = 2 bits
questions.explanationEn: From Slides 36 and 42: Main memory = 16 MB = 2^24 bytes (s + w = 24 bits). Block size = 4 bytes = 2^2 bytes -> Word field w = 2 bits, and s = 24 - 2 = 22 bits. Cache size = 64 KB / 4 bytes per line = 16K = 2^14 lines -> Line field r = 14 bits. Tag field = s - r = 22 - 14 = 8 bits.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 36 và 42: Bộ nhớ chính 16 MB = 2^24 byte => địa chỉ 24 bit. Kích thước block = 4 byte = 2^2 => Word w = 2 bit, phần định danh block s = 24 - 2 = 22 bit. Số dòng cache m = 64 KB / 4 B = 16K = 2^14 dòng => Line r = 14 bit. Vậy Tag = s - r = 22 - 14 = 8 bit.
questions.formula: w = log2(Block_Size); r = log2(Cache_Lines); Tag = Address_Bits - r - w
questions.stepByStep:
1. Address length = log2(16 MB) = 24 bits.
2. Word offset w = log2(4 bytes) = 2 bits.
3. Number of cache lines m = 64 KB / 4 B = 16K = 2^14 -> Line bits r = 14 bits.
4. Tag bits = 24 - 14 - 2 = 8 bits.

questions.subtopic: Fully Associative Mapping Structure
questions.concept: Fully Associative Mapping Address Partitioning (64KB Cache, 4B Block, 16MB Memory)
questions.question: Using the same system (16 MB main memory with 24-bit addresses, 64 KB cache, 4-byte block size), how is the 24-bit memory address partitioned under Fully Associative Mapping (Slide 60), and for hexadecimal address `FFFFFC`, what are the hexadecimal Tag and 2-bit Word values?
options: Tag = 8 bits, Line = 14 bits, Word = 2 bits
Tag = 16 bits, Word = 8 bits
Tag = 14 bits, Word = 10 bits
Tag = 22 bits, Word = 2 bits; for address `FFFFFC` (`1111...1100_2`), Tag = `3FFFFF` hex (shown as `FFFFFC` top 22 bits in Slide 60) and Word = `00_2` (0)
questions.explanationEn: Slide 60 shows that under Fully Associative Mapping, the 24-bit address is divided into a 22-bit Tag field (`s = 22` bits) and a 2-bit Word field (`w = 2` bits), because any main memory block can be placed into any cache line.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 60 (`ch03_CacheMemory.pdf`): Trong ánh xạ liên kết toàn phần (Fully Associative Mapping), địa chỉ 24-bit được chia thành 2 trường: Tag = 22 bit và Word = 2 bit (không có trường Line cố định vì một block có thể nạp vào bất kỳ dòng cache nào).
questions.formula: Tag = s bits = 22 bits; Word = w bits = 2 bits
questions.stepByStep:
1. Address length = 24 bits; Block size = 4 bytes = 2^2 -> Word w = 2 bits.
2. Since any block can occupy any cache line, all remaining s = 24 - 2 = 22 bits form the Tag.

questions.subtopic: k-Way Set-Associative Mapping & 2-Way Simulation
questions.concept: 2-Way Set-Associative Mapping Bit Partitioning & Hex Address Decoding (Slides 69–70)
questions.question: For the same 16 MB main memory (24-bit address) and 64 KB cache (16K lines of 4 bytes each), suppose the cache is organized as a **2-Way Set-Associative Cache** (`k = 2` lines per set, Slides 69–70). How many sets (`v = 2^d`) are in the cache, what are the `(Tag, Set, Word)` bit widths, and for hexadecimal address `1FF 7FFC`, what are the Set number and Tag in hex?
options: 16K (2^14) sets; Tag = 8 bits, Set = 14 bits, Word = 2 bits; Set number = `3FFF` hex
4K (2^12) sets; Tag = 10 bits, Set = 12 bits, Word = 2 bits; Set number = `0FFF` hex
8K (2^13) sets; Tag = 9 bits, Set = 13 bits, Word = 2 bits; for address `1FF 7FFC`, Tag = `0FF` hex (`011111111_2`), Set number = `1FFF` hex, Word = `0` (`00_2`)
32K (2^15) sets; Tag = 7 bits, Set = 15 bits, Word = 2 bits
questions.explanationEn: With m = 16K = 2^14 lines and k = 2 lines/set, the number of sets is v = m / k = 2^14 / 2 = 2^13 = 8K sets -> Set field d = 13 bits. Word field w = 2 bits (4B block). Tag field = s - d = 22 - 13 = 9 bits. On Slide 69–70, hex address `1FF 7FFC` = `0001 1111 1111 0111 1111 1111 1100_2`: the top 9 bits are `000111111_2 = 0FFh` (written as `1FF` in Slide 69's unshifted hex notation), the middle 13 bits are `1 1111 1111 1111_2 = 1FFFh` (Set number), and the bottom 2 bits are `00_2`.
questions.explanationVi: Với 16K = 2^14 dòng chia thành các tập 2 dòng/tập (2-way), số tập là v = 2^14 / 2 = 2^13 = 8K tập => Set d = 13 bit, Word w = 2 bit, và Tag = 24 - 13 - 2 = 9 bit. Với địa chỉ `1FF 7FFC` trên Slide 69–70, 13 bit Set cho giá trị `1FFF` (hex) và 2 bit Word là `00_2`.
questions.formula: v = m / k = 2^d; Tag = s - d; Word = w
questions.stepByStep:
1. Total cache lines m = 16K = 2^14. With k = 2 lines/set, Sets v = 2^14 / 2 = 2^13 -> Set bits d = 13.
2. Word bits w = log2(4) = 2 bits.
3. Tag bits = 24 - 13 - 2 = 9 bits.
4. Binary of 1FF7FFC: 0001 1111 1111 0111 1111 1111 1100 -> 13-bit Set = 1 1111 1111 1111_2 = 1FFFh.

questions.subtopic: k-Way Set-Associative Mapping & 2-Way Simulation
questions.concept: 2-Way Set Associative Cache Simulation Trace (Slide 75)
questions.question: On Slide 75 ('2-Way Set Associative Cache Simulation'), a system has `M = 16` byte addresses (4-bit address: `t=2` tag bits, `s=1` set bit, `b=1` block offset bit), `B = 2` bytes/block, `S = 2` sets, and `E = 2` blocks/set. Starting with an empty cache, the CPU executes the byte-read address trace: `0` (`0000_2`), `1` (`0001_2`), `7` (`0111_2`), `8` (`1000_2`), `0` (`0000_2`). What is the sequence of Hits and Misses for these 5 reads?
options: Read 0: Miss, Read 1: Miss, Read 7: Miss, Read 8: Miss, Read 0: Miss (5 Misses, 0 Hits)
Read 0: Hit, Read 1: Hit, Read 7: Hit, Read 8: Miss, Read 0: Miss (2 Misses, 3 Hits)
Read 0: Miss, Read 1: Hit, Read 7: Miss, Read 8: Miss, Read 0: Miss (because address 8 evicted address 0)
Read 0: Miss, Read 1: Hit, Read 7: Miss, Read 8: Miss, Read 0: Hit (3 Misses, 2 Hits)
questions.explanationEn: Tracing Slide 75: (1) Read 0 (`00_0_0`): Set 0, Tag 00 -> Miss, loads block M[0-1] into Set 0 Way 0. (2) Read 1 (`00_0_1`): Set 0, Tag 00 -> Hit! (spatial locality within M[0-1]). (3) Read 7 (`01_1_1`): Set 1, Tag 01 -> Miss, loads M[6-7] into Set 1 Way 0. (4) Read 8 (`10_0_0`): Set 0, Tag 10 -> Miss, loads M[8-9] into Set 0 Way 1 (since Set 0 has E=2 ways, M[0-1] is NOT evicted!). (5) Read 0 (`00_0_0`): Set 0, Tag 00 -> Hit! (M[0-1] is still in Set 0 Way 0).
questions.explanationVi: Theo mô phỏng trên Slide 75: Đọc 0 (`0000_2`, Set 0, Tag 00) -> Miss (nạp M[0-1] vào Set 0). Đọc 1 (`0001_2`, Set 0, Tag 00) -> Hit (cùng block M[0-1]). Đọc 7 (`0111_2`, Set 1, Tag 01) -> Miss (nạp M[6-7] vào Set 1). Đọc 8 (`1000_2`, Set 0, Tag 10) -> Miss (nạp M[8-9] vào dòng thứ 2 của Set 0, không ghi đè M[0-1] vì cache 2-way). Đọc 0 (`0000_2`, Set 0, Tag 00) -> Hit!
questions.formula: Address = [Tag(2b) | Set(1b) | Offset(1b)]
questions.stepByStep:
1. Addr 0 (00|0|0): Miss -> Set 0 holds {Tag 00: M[0-1]}.
2. Addr 1 (00|0|1): Hit in Set 0 (Tag 00).
3. Addr 7 (01|1|1): Miss -> Set 1 holds {Tag 01: M[6-7]}.
4. Addr 8 (10|0|0): Miss -> Set 0 holds {Tag 00: M[0-1], Tag 10: M[8-9]}.
5. Addr 0 (00|0|0): Hit in Set 0 (Tag 00).

questions.subtopic: LRU, FIFO, LFU & Random Replacement Traces
questions.concept: LRU vs. LFU Page Replacement Trace on 'B E E R B A R E B E A R' (Slides 78–79)
questions.question: Consider the 3-frame memory page trace `B, E, E, R, B, A, R, E, B, E, A, R` shown on Slides 78 (LRU Example) and 79 (LFU Example). After the first 5 references (`B, E, E, R, B`), the 3 frames hold `{B (used at t=1,5; count=2), E (used at t=2,3; count=2), R (used at t=4; count=1)}`. When page `A` is requested at step 6 (`t=6`), which page is evicted under **LRU (Least Recently Used)** vs. **LFU (Least Frequently Used)**?
options: Under both LRU and LFU, page `B` is evicted at step 6
Under LRU, page `R` is evicted; under LFU, page `E` is evicted

Under LRU, page `E` is evicted (since its last use was at t=3, older than R at t=4 and B at t=5); under LFU, page `R` is evicted (since R has the lowest reference count of 1, whereas B and E each have 2 references)
Neither LRU nor LFU evicts any page at step 6 because `A` is a cache hit
questions.explanationEn: At step 6 (`A` arrives), the resident pages are B, E, and R: B was referenced at steps 1 and 5 (most recent = 5, frequency = 2); E was referenced at steps 2 and 3 (most recent = 3, frequency = 2); R was referenced at step 4 (most recent = 4, frequency = 1). Therefore, LRU evicts the least recently used page (`E`, last used at step 3), whereas LFU evicts the least frequently used page (`R`, count = 1).
questions.explanationVi: Tại bước 6 khi nạp trang `A`, 3 khung trang đang chứa: `B` (dùng ở bước 1, 5 -> gần nhất = 5, số lần = 2), `E` (dùng ở bước 2, 3 -> gần nhất = 3, số lần = 2), `R` (dùng ở bước 4 -> gần nhất = 4, số lần = 1). Do đó: Thuật toán LRU thay thế trang lâu nhất chưa dùng là `E` (bước 3); còn thuật toán LFU thay thế trang có số lần truy cập ít nhất là `R` (1 lần).
questions.formula: LRU evicts argmin(last_used_time); LFU evicts argmin(reference_count)
questions.stepByStep:
1. After B, E, E, R, B (steps 1..5): Frame 1=B (last=5, freq=2), Frame 2=E (last=3, freq=2), Frame 3=R (last=4, freq=1).
2. Step 6 requests 'A' (Miss).
3. LRU compares last_used: E(3) < R(4) < B(5) -> evicts E.
4. LFU compares freq: R(1) < B(2)=E(2) -> evicts R.

questions.subtopic: Write-Through vs. Write-Back & Multicore Coherency
questions.concept: Write-Through vs. Write-Back and Cache Coherency Hardware Techniques
questions.question: How do 'Write-Through' and 'Write-Back' cache write policies differ, and what three hardware/system approaches are listed on Slide 83 to prevent cache coherency problems in multiprocessor systems?
options: Write-Through only updates the cache and never writes to RAM; Write-Back writes every byte directly to magnetic tape

Write-Through writes every update to both cache and main memory immediately (generating heavy bus traffic), while Write-Back updates only the cache and sets an UPDATE bit to write back only upon eviction; coherency approaches are (1) Bus Watching with Write-Through, (2) Hardware Transparency, and (3) Non-cacheable Memory
Write-Through uses an UPDATE bit and causes cache coherency problems; Write-Back eliminates all cache coherency issues automatically
Both policies prohibit multiple CPUs from sharing main memory
questions.explanationEn: Slides 81–82 contrast Write-Through (all writes go to main memory and cache so main memory is always valid, but causes heavy traffic) and Write-Back (uses an UPDATE bit, updates main memory only when replaced, minimizing traffic but causing cache coherency challenges). Slide 83 lists the three coherency solutions: Bus Watching with Write Through, Hardware Transparency, and Non-cacheable Memory.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 81–83: Write-Through ghi đồng thời vào cache và bộ nhớ chính (tốn băng thông bus); Write-Back chỉ cập nhật cache kèm bit UPDATE và chỉ ghi về RAM khi dòng cache bị thay thế. Ba giải pháp đồng nhất cache (cache coherency) trên hệ đa xử lý là: Bus Watching with Write Through, Hardware Transparency, và Non-cacheable Memory.

questions.subtopic: Disk Capacity Calculation
questions.concept: Computing Magnetic Disk Capacity (Slide 56 Example)
questions.question:
Calculate the total storage capacity of the magnetic disk in the worked example on Slide 56 (`ch03_Internal_External.pdf`) given:
- `512 bytes/sector`
- `600 sectors/track` (on average)
- `40,000 tracks/surface`
- `2 surfaces/platter`
- `5 platters/disk`
options: 61,440,000,000 bytes (61.44 GB decimal)
12,288,000,000 bytes (12.29 GB decimal)
122,880,000,000 bytes (122.88 GB decimal, or ~114.44 GiB binary)
questions.explanationEn: Using the formula on Slide 56: Capacity = 512 bytes/sector × 600 sectors/track × 40,000 tracks/surface × 2 surfaces/platter × 5 platters/disk = 512 × 600 × 40,000 × 10 = 122,880,000,000 bytes = 122.88 × 10^9 bytes (122.88 GB decimal).
questions.explanationVi: Áp dụng công thức trên Slide 56 (`ch03_Internal_External.pdf`): Dung lượng = 512 × 600 × 40,000 × 2 × 5 = 122,880,000,000 bytes = 122.88 GB (theo hệ thập phân 10^9 B).
questions.formula: Capacity = (bytes/sector) * (sectors/track) * (tracks/surface) * (surfaces/platter) * (platters/disk)
questions.stepByStep:
1. Surfaces per disk = 2 surfaces/platter × 5 platters = 10 surfaces.
2. Tracks per disk = 40,000 × 10 = 400,000 tracks.
3. Sectors per disk = 600 × 400,000 = 240,000,000 sectors.
4. Total bytes = 512 × 240,000,000 = 122,880,000,000 bytes (122.88 GB).

questions.subtopic: Disk Access Time (Seek, Rotational Latency, Transfer)
questions.concept: Calculating Magnetic Disk Access Time (Slide 69 Example)
questions.question: In the worked example on Slide 69 (`ch03_Internal_External.pdf`), a hard disk has a rotational rate of `7200 RPM`, an average seek time `T_avg_seek = 9 ms`, and an average of `600 sectors/track`. What are the average rotational latency (`T_avg_rotation`), the average sector transfer time (`T_avg_transfer`), and the total access time (`T_access`)?
options: T_avg_rotation = 8.33 ms, T_avg_transfer = 1.4 ms, T_access = 18.73 ms
T_avg_rotation = 2.0 ms, T_avg_transfer = 0.5 ms, T_access = 11.5 ms
T_avg_rotation = 4.17 ms (approx 4 ms in slide), T_avg_transfer = 0.014 ms, T_access ≈ 13.18 ms (or 13.014 ms using slide's rounded 4 ms)
T_avg_rotation = 9.0 ms, T_avg_transfer = 4.0 ms, T_access = 22.0 ms
questions.explanationEn: From Slide 68–69: Full rotation time = (60 s / 7200 RPM) × 1000 ms/s = 8.333 ms. Average rotational latency = 1/2 × 8.333 ms = 4.167 ms (rounded to 4 ms on Slide 69). Average transfer time for 1 sector = 8.333 ms / 600 sectors = 0.0139 ms ≈ 0.014 ms. Total access time = 9 ms + 4.167 ms + 0.014 ms = 13.18 ms (or 9 + 4 + 0.014 = 13.014 ms as written on Slide 69).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 68–69: Thời gian quay 1 vòng = (60 / 7200) × 1000 = 8.333 ms. Độ trễ quay trung bình (T_avg_rotation) = 1/2 × 8.333 = 4.17 ms (Slide làm tròn thành 4 ms). Thời gian truyền 1 sector (T_avg_transfer) = 8.333 ms / 600 = 0.014 ms. Tổng thời gian truy cập T_access = 9 + 4 + 0.014 = 13.014 ms (hoặc 13.18 ms nếu giữ 4.17 ms).
questions.formula: T_access = T_seek + 0.5*(60/R)*1000 + (60/R)*(1/sectors_per_track)*1000

questions.subtopic: Platters, Tracks, Sectors, Cylinders, CHS & LBA
questions.concept: Why Operating Systems switched from CHS to LBA (Slides 63–65)
questions.question: Why did modern operating systems replace direct Cylinder-Head-Sector (CHS) addressing with Logical Block Addressing (LBA), according to Slides 64–65 of `ch03_Internal_External.pdf`?
options: CHS was only compatible with Solid-State Drives (SSDs) and could not address magnetic platters
LBA eliminates the need for read/write heads and spindles inside a hard disk

With CHS, the HDD could not hide bad sectors from the OS and the ATA standard with CHS was limited to 8.4 GB disks; with LBA, sectors are identified by a single logical number and the HDD controller internally maps LBA to physical CHS while transparently remapping bad sectors
CHS required a 128-bit address bus
questions.explanationEn: Slides 64–65 explain the two major issues with OS-visible CHS: (1) The HDD cannot hide bad sectors from the operating system, and (2) the old ATA CHS interface could only handle up to 8.4 GB disks. With LBA, the OS supplies a single sector number, and the HDD acts as a black box that maps LBA to physical CHS and hides bad sectors automatically.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 64–65: Khi Hệ điều hành dùng trực tiếp tọa độ vật lý CHS có 2 hạn chế lớn: (1) Ổ cứng không thể tự che giấu các bad sector khỏi OS, và (2) Chuẩn ATA dùng CHS bị giới hạn ở dung lượng 8.4 GB. Với địa chỉ khối logic (LBA), OS chỉ gửi một số thứ tự sector duy nhất, còn bộ điều khiển đĩa tự ánh xạ sang CHS vật lý và tự động loại bỏ các bad sector.

questions.subtopic: SSD Pages/Blocks, FTL & Wear-Leveling
questions.concept: Why Random Writes are Slow on Solid-State Drives (SSDs)
questions.question: According to Slides 76–77 (`ch03_Internal_External.pdf`), why is random write access on an SSD (~300 µs, 14 MB/s) significantly slower than random read access (~30 µs, 140 MB/s)?
options: Because SSDs must physically spin up a magnetic spindle before writing

Because flash memory pages (512B–4KB) can be written only after their entire enclosing block (32–128 pages) is erased (~1 ms), so modifying a single page requires finding/erasing a new block, writing the updated page, and copying all other valid pages from the old block to the new block
Because SSDs use UV light to erase individual bytes over the PCIe bus
Because SSD reads occur in 1 GB chunks while writes occur 1 bit at a time
questions.explanationEn: Slides 76–77 explain that SSD data is read/written in pages (512B–4KB), but a page can be written ONLY after its entire block (32–128 pages) has been erased (which takes around 1 ms). Modifying a page triggers a copy of all useful pages in the block to a newly erased block.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 76–77: Trên ổ cứng SSD, dữ liệu được đọc/ghi theo từng trang (page: 512B–4KB), nhưng một trang chỉ có thể được ghi sau khi toàn bộ khối (block: gồm 32–128 trang) chứa nó đã được xóa (mất khoảng 1 ms). Do đó, việc sửa một trang đòi hỏi phải xóa một khối mới và sao chép toàn bộ các trang hợp lệ khác sang khối mới.

questions.subtopic: RAID Levels 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6
questions.concept: Comparing RAID 0, 1, 4, 5, and 6
questions.question: How does **RAID 5** overcome the write bottleneck of **RAID 4**, and how does **RAID 6** further increase fault tolerance?
options: RAID 4 stores all parity blocks on a single dedicated parity disk (creating a write bottleneck), whereas RAID 5 distributes parity stripes across all disks using round-robin allocation; RAID 6 adds two independent parity calculations (P = Parity and Q = Reed-Solomon) stored on separate blocks across disks, requiring N+2 disks and tolerating the simultaneous loss of 2 disks
RAID 5 uses 100% disk mirroring like RAID 1, while RAID 6 has zero redundancy like RAID 0
RAID 4 uses Hamming codes on bit-level stripes, while RAID 5 requires exactly 5 physical hard drives
RAID 6 requires 3N disks and can only tolerate 1 disk failure
questions.explanationEn: Slides 85–87 explain that RAID 4 uses block-level striping with a single dedicated parity disk (causing a bottleneck on writes). RAID 5 stripes both data and parity across all disks in a round-robin fashion to eliminate the parity-disk bottleneck. RAID 6 performs two separate parity calculations (Parity P and Reed-Solomon Q), requiring N+2 disks and tolerating the loss of up to two disks (so 3 disks must fail for data loss).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 85–87: RAID 4 lưu toàn bộ parity trên 1 đĩa cố định gây nghẽn cổ chai khi ghi; RAID 5 phân tán khối parity đều khắp các đĩa theo kiểu xoay vòng (round-robin); còn RAID 6 dùng 2 mã kiểm tra độc lập (Parity P và Reed-Solomon Q), cần N+2 đĩa và chịu được lỗi hỏng đồng thời 2 đĩa.

options: Mode 1 consists of 12 bytes SYNC + 4 bytes ID (MIN, SEC, Sector, Mode) + 2,048 bytes Data + 288 bytes Layered ECC (total = 2,352 bytes); Mode 2 omits the 288-byte L-ECC to provide 2,336 bytes of user data (12 + 4 + 2,336 = 2,352 bytes)
Mode 1 consists of 512 bytes Data + 1,840 bytes SYNC; Mode 2 consists of 4,096 bytes Data
Mode 1 and Mode 2 both provide 2,352 bytes of pure user data with zero header bytes
Mode 1 uses 1,024 bytes Data + 1,328 bytes ECC; Mode 2 is blank
questions.explanationEn: Figure 6.10 on Slide 93 shows the 2,352-byte CD-ROM block: 12 bytes SYNC + 4 bytes ID + 2,048 bytes Data + 288 bytes L-ECC = 2,352 bytes in Mode 1. Slide 93 notes: Mode 0 = blank data field; Mode 1 = 2048 byte data + error correction; Mode 2 = 2336 byte data (2048 + 288 = 2336).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Hình 6.10 (Slide 93, `ch03_Internal_External.pdf`): Một khối (block) CD-ROM dài 2,352 bytes. Ở Mode 1 (dữ liệu chuẩn có sửa lỗi), khối gồm: 12 bytes SYNC + 4 bytes ID + 2,048 bytes Data + 288 bytes L-ECC = 2,352 bytes. Ở Mode 2, phần L-ECC 288 bytes được gộp vào vùng dữ liệu tạo thành 2,048 + 288 = 2,336 bytes dữ liệu.
questions.formula: Total_Block = 12 (SYNC) + 4 (ID) + 2048 (Data) + 288 (ECC) = 2352 Bytes
questions.stepByStep:

2. In Mode 2, Data + ECC fields combine for user payload: 2048 + 288 = 2336 bytes.

questions.question: A byte-addressable computer has `512 MB` of main memory (`2^29` bytes) and a `1024 KB` **Direct-Mapped** cache with a block (line) size of `64 bytes`. What are the bit widths of the `(Tag, Line, Word)` fields in the 29-bit memory address?
options: Tag = 11 bits, Line = 12 bits, Word = 6 bits
Tag = 14 bits, Line = 9 bits, Word = 6 bits
Tag = 11 bits, Line = 13 bits, Word = 5 bits
Tag = 9 bits, Line = 14 bits, Word = 6 bits
questions.explanationEn: Address length = log2(512 MB) = 29 bits. Block size = 64 B = 2^6 -> Word offset w = 6 bits. Cache lines m = 1024 KB / 64 B = 2^14 lines -> Line field r = 14 bits. Tag field = 29 - 14 - 6 = 9 bits.
questions.explanationVi: Địa chỉ bộ nhớ chính 512 MB có 29 bit. Block 64 B = 2^6 => Word w = 6 bit. Số dòng cache m = 1024 KB / 64 B = 2^14 => Line r = 14 bit. Vậy Tag = 29 - 14 - 6 = 9 bit.
questions.formula: w = log2(Block_Size); r = log2(Cache_Size / Block_Size); Tag = Addr_Bits - r - w
questions.stepByStep:
1. Total address bits = log2(512 × 2^20) = 29 bits.
2. Word bits w = log2(64) = 6 bits.
3. Cache lines m = (1024 × 2^10) / 64 = 2^14 -> r = 14 bits.
4. Tag bits = 29 - 14 - 6 = 9 bits.

questions.question: A magnetic hard disk rotates at `5400 RPM`, has an average seek time of `10.0 ms`, and has `500 sectors per track`. What are its average rotational latency (`T_avg_rotation`), single-sector transfer time (`T_avg_transfer`), and total average access time (`T_access`)?
options: T_rotation = 11.12 ms, T_transfer = 0.220 ms, T_access = 21.12 ms
T_rotation = 5.00 ms, T_transfer = 1.000 ms, T_access = 16.00 ms
T_rotation = 5.56 ms, T_transfer = 5.560 ms, T_access = 21.12 ms
T_rotation = 5.56 ms, T_transfer = 0.022 ms, T_access = 15.58 ms
questions.explanationEn: Full rotation = (60 / 5400) × 1000 ms = 11.11 ms. Average rotational latency = 0.5 × 11.11 = 5.56 ms. Sector transfer time = 11.11 ms / 500 = 0.022 ms. Total access time = 10.0 + 5.56 + 0.022 = 15.58 ms.
questions.explanationVi: Chu kỳ quay 1 vòng = (60 / 5400) × 1000 = 11.11 ms. Độ trễ quay trung bình = 1/2 × 11.11 = 5.56 ms. Thời gian truyền 1 sector = 11.11 / 500 = 0.022 ms. Tổng thời gian truy cập = 15.58 ms.
questions.formula: T_access = T_seek + 0.5*(60000/RPM) + (60000/RPM)/Sectors_Per_Track

questions.subtopic: Word Alignment & Byte Ordering (Big-Endian vs. Little-Endian)
questions.concept: Byte Ordering in Memory for 32-bit value 0x1A2B3C4D
questions.question: A 32-bit word `0x1A2B3C4D` is written to byte-addressable memory starting at address `0x0000`. What byte values (in hex) reside at the four consecutive addresses (`+0, +1, +2, +3`) on a **Little-Endian** machine vs. a **Big-Endian** machine?
options: Little-Endian: `1A, 2B, 3C, 4D`; Big-Endian: `4D, 3C, 2B, 1A`
Little-Endian: `3C, 4D, 1A, 2B`; Big-Endian: `2B, 1A, 4D, 3C`
Both machines store `1A, 2B, 3C, 4D`
Little-Endian: `4D, 3C, 2B, 1A`; Big-Endian: `1A, 2B, 3C, 4D`
questions.explanationEn: In Little-Endian, the Least Significant Byte (`4D`) is placed at the lowest address (`0x0000`), giving `4D, 3C, 2B, 1A`. In Big-Endian, the Most Significant Byte (`1A`) is placed at the lowest address, giving `1A, 2B, 3C, 4D`.
questions.explanationVi: Với Little-Endian, byte thấp nhất (`4D`) đặt tại địa chỉ thấp nhất (`0x0000`): `4D, 3C, 2B, 1A`. Với Big-Endian, byte cao nhất (`1A`) đặt tại địa chỉ thấp nhất: `1A, 2B, 3C, 4D`.
questions.formula: Little-Endian: Addr[0] = LSB; Big-Endian: Addr[0] = MSB
questions.stepByStep:
1. Split 0x1A2B3C4D into 4 bytes: MSB=1A, 2B, 3C, LSB=4D.
2. Little-Endian orders LSB -> MSB: 4D, 3C, 2B, 1A.
3. Big-Endian orders MSB -> LSB: 1A, 2B, 3C, 4D.

Internal memory transfers data in magnetic cylinders, while external memory transfers data in flip-flops
questions.explanationEn: Slide 12 defines Unit of Transfer (Internal: equal to number of data lines into/out of memory module; External: transferred in blocks larger than a word) and Addressable Unit (Smallest location which can be uniquely addressed—word/byte internally, cluster on magnetic disks).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 12: Đơn vị truyền (Unit of Transfer) với bộ nhớ trong bằng số đường dữ liệu vào/ra mô-đun nhớ, còn với bộ nhớ ngoài là các khối (block); Đơn vị định địa chỉ (Addressable unit) là vị trí nhỏ nhất có địa chỉ duy nhất (word/byte trong RAM, cluster/sector trên đĩa từ).

questions.subtopic: Word Alignment & Byte Ordering (Big-Endian vs. Little-Endian)
questions.concept: Word-Oriented Memory Addressing (32-bit vs. 64-bit words)
questions.question: In a byte-addressable memory organized into aligned words (Slide 10 of `ch03_Internal_External.pdf`), the address of a word is the address of its first byte, and addresses of successive words differ by the word size in bytes. What are the byte addresses (in decimal) of Word 0, Word 1, Word 2, and Word 10 for a **32-bit (4-byte)** word system versus a **64-bit (8-byte)** word system?
options: 32-bit words: 0, 32, 64, and 320; 64-bit words: 0, 64, 128, and 640
32-bit words: 0, 1, 2, and 10; 64-bit words: 0, 2, 4, and 20
32-bit words: 0, 4, 8, and 40; 64-bit words: 0, 8, 16, and 80
32-bit words: 4, 8, 12, and 44; 64-bit words: 8, 16, 24, and 88
questions.explanationEn: Slide 10 shows that 32-bit words are 4 bytes wide, so Word k is at byte address 4 × k (Word 0 = 0, Word 1 = 4, Word 2 = 8, Word 10 = 40). For 64-bit words (8 bytes wide), Word k is at byte address 8 × k (Word 0 = 0, Word 1 = 8, Word 2 = 16, Word 10 = 80).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 10 (`ch03_Internal_External.pdf`): Từ 32-bit dài 4 byte nên địa chỉ của từ thứ k là 4×k (Word 0=0, Word 1=4, Word 2=8, Word 10=40). Từ 64-bit dài 8 byte nên địa chỉ của từ thứ k là 8×k (Word 0=0, Word 1=8, Word 2=16, Word 10=80).
questions.formula: Address(Word_k) = k * (Word_Bits / 8)
questions.stepByStep:
1. 32-bit word = 4 bytes -> Word 10 is at 10 × 4 = 40.
2. 64-bit word = 8 bytes -> Word 10 is at 10 × 8 = 80.

questions.subtopic: 2D DRAM Bank, Supercells & RAS/CAS Pin Multiplexing
questions.concept: Two-Phase DRAM Supercell Read Operation (RAS and CAS)
questions.question: In the two-phase reading of a DRAM supercell `(row=2, col=1)` on a `16 × 8` DRAM chip (Slides 36–37 of `ch03_Internal_External.pdf`), what occurs during Step 1 (`RAS`) and Step 2 (`CAS`)?
options: Step 1: Row Access Strobe (RAS=2) activates row 2 via the row decoder, and the sense amplifiers copy all supercells of row 2 into the internal row buffer; Step 2: Column Access Strobe (CAS=1) selects column 1 from the internal row buffer via the column multiplexer and drives supercell (2,1) onto the data lines
Step 1: CAS selects column 1; Step 2: RAS erases the entire DRAM bank
Step 1: The CPU reads directly from the capacitor without sense amplifiers; Step 2: The CPU rewrites the BIOS
RAS and CAS are asserted simultaneously on separate 64-bit address buses
questions.explanationEn: Slides 32 and 36–37 illustrate the two-phase DRAM read: Step 1(a) Row Access Strobe (RAS) selects row 2; Step 1(b) row 2 is copied from the DRAM array to the internal row buffer via sense amplifiers. Step 2(a) Column Access Strobe (CAS) selects column 1; Step 2(b) supercell (2,1) is copied from the row buffer to the data lines back to the CPU.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 32 và 36–37: Bước 1 (RAS): chọn hàng 2 và sao chép toàn bộ hàng 2 vào bộ đệm hàng nội bộ (internal row buffer) qua bộ khuếch đại cảm biến (sense amplifiers). Bước 2 (CAS): chọn cột 1 từ bộ đệm hàng để xuất ô nhớ (2,1) ra đường dữ liệu về CPU.

questions.subtopic: SDRAM, DDR1/DDR2/DDR3 Prefetch & Memory Modules
questions.concept: Enhanced DRAMs: SDRAM and DDR1/DDR2/DDR3 Prefetch Multipliers
questions.question: How does Synchronous DRAM (SDRAM) improve upon asynchronous DRAM, and how do DDR1, DDR2, and DDR3 SDRAM scale data transfer rates relative to a single-data-rate (SDR = `n B/sec`) array at clock frequency `f` (Slides 39–40)?
options: SDRAM eliminates capacitors; DDR1 is 10× faster, DDR2 is 100× faster, and DDR3 is 1,000× faster
DDR1, DDR2, and DDR3 only operate on magnetic disks

SDRAM uses a conventional clock signal instead of asynchronous control and allows reuse of row addresses (e.g., RAS followed by multiple CAS, CAS, CAS); DDR1 transfers at 2× (`2n B/sec`), DDR2 at 4× (`4n B/sec`), and DDR3 at 8× (`8n B/sec`)
SDRAM requires a separate RAS for every single bit within the same row
questions.explanationEn: Slides 39–40 explain that SDRAM uses a conventional clock signal and allows reuse of row addresses (RAS, CAS, CAS, CAS). Double data-rate synchronous DRAM (DDR SDRAM) increases the I/O buffer width/rate: DDR1 is twice as fast (2n B/sec), DDR2 is four times as fast (4n B/sec), and DDR3 is eight times as fast (8n B/sec).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 39–40: SDRAM dùng xung nhịp đồng bộ và cho phép tái sử dụng địa chỉ hàng (1 lần RAS kèm nhiều lần CAS liên tiếp). DDR1 tăng tốc gấp 2 lần (2n B/s), DDR2 gấp 4 lần (4n B/s), và DDR3 gấp 8 lần (8n B/s).

questions.subtopic: SDRAM, DDR1/DDR2/DDR3 Prefetch & Memory Modules
questions.concept: Combining 8Mx8 DRAM Chips into a 64 MB Memory Module (Slides 38, 44)
questions.question: In the 64 MB DRAM Memory Module shown on Slides 38 and 44 (`ch03_Internal_External.pdf`), eight `8M × 8-bit` DRAM chips (`DRAM 0` through `DRAM 7`) are combined to form a 64-bit doubleword wide module (`8 × 8 = 64 bits`). How are the command/bank/address lines and the data lines connected across the 8 chips, and what is the effect on throughput and delay?
options: Data lines are shared on a single 8-bit bus while address lines are concatenated; delay increases 8× and throughput stays the same

Command, bank-selection, and address lines are shared across all 8 chips (each chip receives the same row/col command), while the 8-bit data lines of the 8 chips are concatenated into a 64-bit bus; throughput increases 8× while access delay remains the same
Each chip executes independent CPU instructions; throughput increases 64×
Only 1 chip is active at a time while the other 7 chips are powered off
questions.explanationEn: Slide 44 states: 'A memory module consists of DRAM chips. Command lines, bank selection lines, address lines: shared. Data lines: concatenated (8x8 = 64 bit wide). Each chip receives all commands. Effect: Throughput increases 8x; Delay: the same.'
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 38 và 44: Trên thanh RAM gồm 8 chip `8M × 8-bit`, các đường lệnh, chọn bank và địa chỉ được dùng chung (shared), còn 8 đường dữ liệu của mỗi chip được ghép nối tiếp (concatenated) tạo thành bus 64-bit (8×8=64). Kết quả: Băng thông (throughput) tăng 8 lần trong khi độ trễ (delay) giữ nguyên.

questions.subtopic: Low-Order, High-Order & Mixed Memory Interleaving
questions.concept: Low-Order Cyclic Memory Interleaving (Slide 45–46)
questions.question: A memory system uses **Low-Order Bit (Cyclic) Interleaving** across `B = 4` banks (`Bank 0, Bank 1, Bank 2, Bank 3`), where memory word address `A` maps to bank `b = A mod 4` and word offset within the bank `w = A div 4` (Slides 45–46). To which bank `b` and word index `w` does word address `A = 23` map, and why does low-order interleaving speed up sequential array accesses?
options: Bank b = 3 (since 23 mod 4 = 3) and word index w = 5 (since 23 div 4 = 5); consecutive addresses (0, 1, 2, 3...) fall in different banks so accesses to the 4 banks can be staged/overlapped over time on the memory bus
Bank b = 5 and word index w = 3; all consecutive addresses fall in Bank 0
Bank b = 0 and word index w = 23; only 1 bank can be active per second
Bank b = 2 and word index w = 4
questions.explanationEn: Using Slide 45–46: For A = 23 and B = 4 banks, b = 23 mod 4 = 3 (Bank 3) and w = 23 div 4 = 5 (Word 5 in Bank 3; verified in the table on Slide 46 where Bank 3 lists 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23 at index 5). Consecutive addresses map to different banks, allowing bank accesses to overlap.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 45–46: Với B = 4 bank và địa chỉ A = 23, chỉ số bank b = 23 mod 4 = 3 (Bank 3) và vị trí từ trong bank w = 23 div 4 = 5. Các địa chỉ liên tiếp nằm ở các bank khác nhau nên có thể truy cập gối đầu nhau để tăng băng thông.
questions.formula: b = A mod B; w = A div B
questions.stepByStep:
1. Divide A = 23 by B = 4: quotient w = 23 // 4 = 5, remainder b = 23 % 4 = 3.
2. Thus A = 23 is in Bank 3 at word offset 5.

questions.subtopic: Cache Hit/Miss Operations & (S, E, B) Organization
questions.concept: System Bus Traffic on Cache Hit vs. Cache Miss (Slide 25)
questions.question: When the CPU reads a word from memory and a **Cache Hit** occurs (Slide 25 of `ch03_CacheMemory.pdf`), what happens to the data and address buffers connecting the cache to the system bus?
options: The data and address buffers to the system bus are disabled, and communication occurs exclusively between the processor and the cache with zero system bus traffic
The cache broadcasts the hit data across the entire system bus to all I/O devices
Main memory is still read in parallel and overwrites the cache line
The CPU halts for 100 clock cycles to refresh the SRAM
questions.explanationEn: Slide 25 states: 'When a cache hit occurs, the data and address buffers are disabled and the communication is only between processor and cache with no system bus traffic.'
questions.explanationVi: Slide 25 (`ch03_CacheMemory.pdf`) nêu rõ: Khi xảy ra Cache Hit, các bộ đệm dữ liệu và địa chỉ nối ra bus hệ thống bị ngắt (disabled), việc truyền thông chỉ diễn ra trực tiếp giữa CPU và Cache mà không phát sinh lưu lượng trên bus hệ thống.

questions.subtopic: Direct Mapping Address Structure & Hex Examples
questions.concept: Primary Disadvantage of Direct Mapping (Conflict Thrashing)
questions.question: While Direct Mapping is simple and inexpensive to implement in hardware, what is its primary performance drawback noted on Slide 47?
options: It requires searching every cache line tag simultaneously using expensive associative comparators
It cannot support cache blocks larger than 1 bit
It requires flushing the entire cache on every arithmetic instruction

Each main memory block has a fixed cache location (i = j mod m), so if a program repeatedly accesses two blocks that map to the exact same cache line, they continually evict each other (thrashing) and cache misses are very high
questions.explanationEn: Slide 47 summarizes Direct Mapping: 'Simple, Inexpensive, Fixed location for given block: If a program accesses 2 blocks that map to the same line repeatedly, cache misses are very high.'
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 47: Nhược điểm chính của ánh xạ trực tiếp (Direct Mapping) là mỗi block bộ nhớ chính chỉ được ánh xạ vào một dòng cache cố định; nếu chương trình truy cập lặp đi lặp lại 2 block cùng ánh xạ vào một dòng cache thì chúng sẽ liên tục đẩy nhau ra (conflict miss cao).

questions.subtopic: LRU, FIFO, LFU & Random Replacement Traces
questions.concept: Hardware Implementation of LRU in a 2-Way Set Associative Cache (Slide 77)
questions.question: According to Slide 77 ('Replacement algorithm'), how is the Least Recently Used (LRU) algorithm efficiently implemented in hardware for a **2-Way Set Associative** cache?
options: By maintaining a 64-bit floating-point timestamp register for every byte in main memory
By calling an operating system interrupt handler on every cache hit

By maintaining a single `USE` bit for each of the two lines in a set: when a block is referenced or read into a line, its `USE` bit is set to 1 and the other line's `USE` bit in that set is set to 0; upon eviction, the line whose `USE` bit is 0 is replaced
By sorting all cache lines alphabetically every millisecond
questions.explanationEn: Slide 77 explains: 'Implementation: with 2-way set associative, have a USE bit for each line in a set. When a block is read into cache, use the line whose USE bit is set to 0, then set its USE bit to one, and the other line's USE bit to 0.'
questions.explanationVi: Slide 77 giải thích cách cài đặt phần cứng LRU cho cache 2-way: Mỗi dòng trong tập (set) có 1 bit `USE`. Khi một dòng được truy cập hoặc nạp mới, bit `USE` của nó được đặt bằng 1 và bit `USE` của dòng còn lại trong tập đặt bằng 0. Khi cần thay thế, dòng có `USE = 0` sẽ được chọn.

questions.subtopic: Platters, Tracks, Sectors, Cylinders, CHS & LBA
questions.concept: Magnetic Disk Geometry: Tracks, Sectors, Cylinders, and Recording Zones
questions.question: In magnetic disk organization (Slides 53–55 and 60–62 of `ch03_Internal_External.pdf`), what is a 'cylinder', why do modern disks partition tracks into 'recording zones', and why can individual bits NOT be modified in-place without reading/writing a whole sector?
options: A cylinder is a single 512-byte sector; all tracks from center to edge must have the exact same circumference

A cylinder is the set of aligned tracks at the same radial position across all platter surfaces; recording zones allow outer tracks (with larger circumference) to hold more sectors per track than inner tracks; and because bits are encoded by changes in magnetic field direction, modifying a single bit would alter the magnetic field direction of subsequent bit positions, so whole sectors (512B) must be read/written
Recording zones are used only on magnetic tape; individual bits can be modified independently by the ALU
A cylinder refers to the spindle motor's ball bearings
questions.explanationEn: Slide 54 defines a cylinder as aligned tracks across platters; Slide 55 explains recording zones (disjoint subsets of tracks where each zone has a different number of sectors/track based on the innermost track circumference of that zone); Slide 60 explains that because reading detects changes in the magnetic field, individual bits cannot be modified without changing subsequent bit positions, so only whole sectors are read/written.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 54–55 và 60: Trụ (Cylinder) là tập hợp các rãnh (track) có cùng bán kính trên mọi mặt đĩa; Vùng ghi (Recording zones) chia các rãnh thành từng nhóm để các rãnh phía ngoài chứa được nhiều sector hơn rãnh phía trong; và vì bit 1/0 được mã hóa bằng sự đổi chiều từ trường nên không thể sửa lẻ từng bit mà phải đọc/ghi nguyên cả sector.

questions.subtopic: Platters, Tracks, Sectors, Cylinders, CHS & LBA
questions.concept: Components of a Magnetic Disk Sector (Slides 61–62)
questions.question: According to the sector diagram on Slides 61–62 (`ch03_Internal_External.pdf`), what are the components surrounding and inside a magnetic disk sector (`Gap`, `Preamble`, `Data`, `CRC/ECC`, `Flush pad`) and their purposes?
options: Preamble erases the platter; Gap stores the operating system kernel; Flush pad cools the spindle

Gap leaves time to switch the read/write head on and off; Preamble calibrates the head (adjusts signal strength and data density) and marks the start of data; Data holds the sector payload (typically 512B); CRC/ECC provides error detection/correction; and Flush pad leaves time for the last bytes to leave the head
CRC/ECC calibrates rotational speed; Preamble stores user files
A sector contains only 512 bytes of data with no gaps, headers, or error-correction fields
questions.explanationEn: Slides 61–62 detail the components of a sector: Gap (time to switch on/off read or write head), Preamble (calibrates head—adjusts signal strength and data density—and indicates start of data), Data (512 bytes), CRC/ECC, and Flush pad (time for last bytes to leave the head).
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 61–62: Một sector trên đĩa từ gồm: Gap (khoảng trống để bật/tắt đầu đọc/ghi), Preamble (đồng bộ và hiệu chỉnh cường độ tín hiệu/mật độ dữ liệu), Data (dữ liệu 512B), CRC/ECC (kiểm tra và sửa lỗi), và Flush pad (đệm thời gian cho các byte cuối rời đầu từ).

questions.subtopic: Platters, Tracks, Sectors, Cylinders, CHS & LBA
questions.concept: Reading a Disk Sector via DMA and Interrupts (Slides 73–75)
questions.question: In the 3-step 'Reading a disk sector' sequence illustrated on Slides 73–75 (`ch03_Internal_External.pdf`), how do the CPU, Disk Controller, Main Memory, and I/O Bus interact?
options: (1) The CPU initiates the disk read by writing the command, logical block number (LBA), and destination memory address to the disk controller's I/O ports; (2) The disk controller reads the sector and performs a Direct Memory Access (DMA) transfer directly into main memory over the bus; (3) When the DMA transfer completes, the disk controller notifies the CPU by asserting an interrupt signal
(1) The disk controller halts the CPU clock; (2) The CPU reads each bit manually from the platter; (3) Main memory sends an interrupt to the disk
(1) The CPU copies the sector from L1 cache to the disk; (2) The USB controller formats the disk; (3) The monitor displays the DMA address
(1) The disk controller writes the sector directly into the CPU's Program Counter without using main memory
questions.explanationEn: Slides 73–75 show the exact 3 steps: (1) CPU initiates disk read by writing command, logical block number, and destination memory address to a port associated with the disk controller; (2) Disk controller reads the sector and performs a DMA transfer into main memory; (3) When the DMA transfer completes, the disk controller notifies the CPU with an interrupt.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 73–75: Quy trình đọc 1 sector đĩa gồm 3 bước: (1) CPU khởi tạo bằng cách ghi lệnh, số khối logic (LBA) và địa chỉ đích trong RAM tới cổng của bộ điều khiển đĩa; (2) Bộ điều khiển đĩa đọc sector và truyền trực tiếp vào bộ nhớ chính qua DMA; (3) Khi truyền DMA hoàn tất, bộ điều khiển đĩa phát tín hiệu ngắt (interrupt) báo cho CPU.

questions.subtopic: RAID Levels 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6
questions.concept: RAID Usable Capacity and Fault Tolerance Calculation
questions.question: A storage architect has `6 identical hard disks`, each with a capacity of `2 TB` (total raw capacity = `12 TB`). What is the usable data capacity and maximum number of simultaneous disk failures tolerated without data loss if the array is configured as **RAID 0**, **RAID 1**, **RAID 5**, or **RAID 6**?
options: RAID 0: 6 TB usable; RAID 1: 12 TB usable; RAID 5: 12 TB usable; RAID 6: 10 TB usable
RAID 0: 10 TB usable; RAID 1: 8 TB usable; RAID 5: 6 TB usable; RAID 6: 4 TB usable
All four RAID levels provide 12 TB usable capacity and tolerate 2 disk failures

RAID 0: 12 TB usable (0 disk failures tolerated); RAID 1: 6 TB usable (1 disk per mirrored pair tolerated); RAID 5: 10 TB usable (1 disk failure tolerated); RAID 6: 8 TB usable (2 disk failures tolerated)
questions.explanationEn: With N = 6 disks of 2 TB each: RAID 0 stripes across all 6 disks with no redundancy -> 6 × 2 = 12 TB usable, 0 failures tolerated. RAID 1 mirrors pairs of disks (50% capacity) -> 3 × 2 = 6 TB usable. RAID 5 uses 1 disk's worth of distributed parity (N - 1 = 5 data disks equivalent) -> 5 × 2 = 10 TB usable, tolerates 1 disk failure. RAID 6 uses 2 disks' worth of dual parity (N - 2 = 4 data disks equivalent) -> 4 × 2 = 8 TB usable, tolerates 2 disk failures.
questions.explanationVi: Với 6 ổ đĩa 2 TB (tổng dung lượng thô 12 TB): RAID 0 dùng 100% dung lượng = 12 TB (không chịu lỗi); RAID 1 soi gương 50% = 6 TB; RAID 5 mất dung lượng tương đương 1 ổ cho parity phân tán => còn (6-1)×2 = 10 TB (chịu lỗi 1 ổ); RAID 6 mất dung lượng tương đương 2 ổ cho parity kép P+Q => còn (6-2)×2 = 8 TB (chịu lỗi 2 ổ).
questions.formula: RAID0 = N*C; RAID1 = (N/2)*C; RAID5 = (N-1)*C; RAID6 = (N-2)*C
questions.stepByStep:
1. N = 6 disks, C = 2 TB.
2. RAID 0 = 6 × 2 = 12 TB (0 fault tolerance).
3. RAID 1 = (6 / 2) × 2 = 6 TB.
4. RAID 5 = (6 - 1) × 2 = 10 TB (1 disk fault tolerance).
5. RAID 6 = (6 - 2) × 2 = 8 TB (2 disk fault tolerance).

questions.subtopic: Optical Storage (CD-ROM, DVD, Blu-ray) & 2352-Byte Sector Format
questions.concept: Comparing CD-ROM, DVD, and Blu-ray Optical Storage Technologies (Table 6.6)
questions.question: According to Table 6.6 ('Optical Disk Products', Slide 89) and Slides 90–92 of `ch03_Internal_External.pdf`, how are binary 1s and 0s physically represented on a CD-ROM, and what are the maximum storage capacities of a standard CD-ROM, a double-sided dual-layer DVD, and a single-layer Blu-ray disk?
options: CD-ROMs use concentric magnetic rings spinning at 15,000 RPM; capacities are 100 GB for CD-ROM and 1 MB for Blu-ray
CD-ROMs store data in 6-transistor SRAM cells; DVD uses an infrared 900-nm laser for 500 TB capacity
Blu-ray disks can only store analog vinyl audio

Binary 1s are defined by the transitions between pits and lands (and 0s by constant pit/land regions) along a single spiral track read by a constant linear velocity laser; capacities are ~650–680 MB for CD-ROM, up to 17 GB for DVD (8.54 GB single-sided dual-layer), and 25 GB per single-sided layer for Blu-ray (using a 405-nm blue-violet laser)
questions.explanationEn: Slides 89–92 explain: CD-ROM records data in a single spiral track from the center outward (~5 miles long if unraveled) at constant linear velocity, where transitions between pits and lands define binary ones. Capacities: CD-ROM holds >650 MB; DVD holds 8.54 GB (single-sided quad-density) and up to 17 GB (double-sided); Blu-ray uses a 405-nm blue-violet laser to store 25 GB on a single layer.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 89–92: Đĩa quang CD-ROM ghi dữ liệu trên một rãnh xoắn ốc duy nhất từ tâm ra ngoài với tốc độ dài không đổi (constant linear velocity), trong đó sự chuyển tiếp giữa hố (pit) và bề mặt phẳng (land) biểu diễn bit 1. Dung lượng: CD-ROM ~650 MB; DVD tối đa 8.54 GB (1 mặt) đến 17 GB (2 mặt); Blu-ray dùng tia laser xanh tím 405-nm đạt 25 GB trên 1 lớp.

questions.subtopic: Cache Hit/Miss Operations & (S, E, B) Organization
questions.concept: General Cache Organization (S, E, B) Total Data Capacity
questions.question: In the General Cache Organization `(S, E, B)` diagram on Slide 23 (`ch03_CacheMemory.pdf`), a cache has `S = 2^s` sets, `E` lines per set, and `B = 2^b` data bytes per cache block, plus `1 valid bit` and `t = m - (s + b)` tag bits per line (where `m` is the physical address width). If `m = 32 bits`, `s = 10` (`S = 1024 sets`), `E = 4 lines/set`, and `b = 6` (`B = 64 bytes/block`), what is the cache's usable **data capacity** (`C = S × E × B`) and how many total overhead bits (`valid + tag`) are stored across all cache lines?
options: Data capacity C = 64 KB; Tag t = 10 bits
Data capacity C = 256 KB (262,144 bytes); Tag t = 16 bits + 1 valid bit = 17 overhead bits/line × 4,096 lines = 69,632 overhead bits (8.5 KB)
Data capacity C = 1 MB; Tag t = 32 bits
Data capacity C = 16 KB; Tag t = 6 bits
questions.explanationEn: From Slide 23: Number of sets S = 2^10 = 1024. Total cache lines = S × E = 1024 × 4 = 4,096 lines. Block size B = 2^6 = 64 bytes. Usable data capacity C = S × E × B = 4,096 × 64 bytes = 262,144 bytes = 256 KB. Tag width t = 32 - (10 + 6) = 16 bits. Each line has 1 valid bit + 16 tag bits = 17 overhead bits; across 4,096 lines, total overhead = 4,096 × 17 = 69,632 bits = 8.5 KB.
questions.explanationVi: Theo Slide 23: Số tập S = 2^10 = 1024; số dòng trên mỗi tập E = 4 => tổng số dòng = 4,096 dòng. Kích thước mỗi khối B = 2^6 = 64 bytes => Dung lượng dữ liệu C = S × E × B = 4,096 × 64 = 256 KB. Số bit Tag t = 32 - (10 + 6) = 16 bit. Cộng thêm 1 bit Valid là 17 bit phụ trội/dòng × 4,096 dòng = 69,632 bit (8.5 KB).
questions.formula: C = S * E * B; t = m - (s + b); Overhead_Bits = S * E * (1 + t)
questions.stepByStep:
1. Compute S = 2^10 = 1024 sets and B = 2^6 = 64 bytes/block.
2. Total lines = S × E = 1024 × 4 = 4096 lines.
3. Data capacity C = 4096 × 64 B = 256 KB.
4. Tag bits t = 32 - 10 - 6 = 16 bits; overhead = 4096 × (16 + 1) = 69,632 bits.
